overview: This file brings together U.S. consular reporting and interdepartmental correspondence on Taiwan’s petroleum and natural-gas industry under Japanese rule. It contains a brief 1931 report of an oil strike at Kinsui; John B. Ketcham’s detailed April 1932 survey of oil fields, gasoline and carbon-black production, trade statistics, Japanese government support, naval reservations, and foreign competition; appreciative letters from U.S. naval and commercial-intelligence officials; and a July 1932 reassessment showing that production had fallen despite highly optimistic press reports. A September memorandum dismisses the later report as of little interest to the Far Eastern Division, while a 1944 charge slip records subsequent circulation of enclosures from the file.

subfiles.title: Recent Developments in the Taiwan Petroleum Industry
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State; copy to the Consulate General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Surveys Taiwan’s oil and natural-gas fields, petroleum-product output and trade, carbon-black manufacture, and the competitive position of foreign oil companies.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham describes Taiwan as the Japanese Empire’s principal domestic source of gasoline and details Japan Oil Company operations at Kinsui, Shukkoko, and Gyunikuki, including new gas wells and planned processing capacity. Statistical tables cover gasoline, crude petroleum, kerosene, lubricants, and liquid fuel production, consumption, imports, and exports. The report also examines government subsidies, areas reserved for the Japanese Navy, American-supplied processing equipment, expanding carbon-black production, and growing pressure on foreign petroleum companies. Its confidential section identifies Standard Oil Company of New York and Texas Oil Corporation and states that much of the information came from an undisclosed source because the Government-General of Taiwan released no petroleum information.

subfiles.title: Report on declining petroleum production in Taiwan
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State; copies to U.S. commercial, consular, and naval officers at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Revises earlier forecasts after production statistics showed that Taiwan’s petroleum and gasoline output declined in the first half of 1932.
subfiles.summary: The confidential report compares production during January–June 1932 with the same period in 1931 and finds declines in crude oil, kerosene, and gasoline, including gasoline manufactured from natural gas. Ketcham argues that widely publicized reports of new Kinsui and Gyunikuki gas gushers were grossly exaggerated and suggests they may have been intended to raise Japan Oil Company’s share price before its annual meeting. The report also records imports of Japanese gasoline for blending, declining exports to Japan, and a modest rise in local consumption. It reduces the estimated 1932 gasoline output from ten million to no more than eight million gallons and identifies an official of a foreign oil company as the source of the production figures.

interest: Shows an optimistic Taiwan oil survey corrected by confidential figures, and consular reporting valued by State, Navy, and Commerce.
